absolute_simultaneity_positive: The duration between two events is a quantity intrinsic to those events, and cannot depend upon the accidental circumstances of the observer who measures it.
When a signal departs from one station and arrives at another, the interval of its passage is a fixed and definite magnitude, whatever the motion of any witness.
It is manifest that the present moment extends across the whole of nature, embracing alike the distant nebulae and the affairs of our own laboratory.
Two occurrences separated by a wide tract of space nevertheless possess a determinate order in time, and this order is common to every rational observer.
The instant at which a distant star suffers a certain change is as definite a moment as the instant of our observing it, though the two be not the same.
Should we admit that time itself were variable with the observer, the very notion of a common history of the universe must dissolve into unintelligibility.
The propagation of light across a measured interval consumes a definite duration, independent of any velocity possessed by the source or by the recipient.
Whenever two events occur, there subsists between them a relation of before, after, or together, which no change of station or motion can alter.
The clocks of Greenwich and of Paris, once properly regulated, indicate the same instant, and this coincidence is a fact of nature, not a stipulation of art.
There belongs to the very idea of an event that it should occupy a moment in the universal time, common to all observers whatsoever.
If we suppose two flashes to be produced together, they are together for all who behold them, whether the beholders be at rest or in swift motion.
Duration is no less objective a feature of the physical world than extension, and to relativise it would be to abandon the intelligibility of mechanics.
The synchronism of two remote pendulums, once established by careful comparison, is a real relation between them, and not a mere conventional posit.
Every physical process, wherever situated, may be referred to a single scale of moments, upon which the whole succession of natural events is inscribed.
That two occurrences at widely sundered places should happen at the same instant is a fact capable of being determined with any degree of exactness we please.
The passage of an interval of time is the same for the traveller upon the swiftest vehicle as for him who remains stationary in his study.
One cannot maintain without absurdity that the very order of events, or the length of their duration, should be dependent upon the motion of the spectator.
To speak of an event as occurring is to imply its place in the universal time, which comprehends all things in one comprehensive succession.
The velocity of light across the ether, being a natural constant, permits us to compute the exact instant of a distant occurrence from the instant of its perception.
Were two lightning-strokes to fall simultaneously upon two distant mountains, this simultaneity would be an objective circumstance, discoverable in principle by every observer.
relativity_of_simultaneity_negative: What is called the simultaneity of two separated events is no absolute matter, but subsists only in reference to a system of clocks conventionally regulated together.
Two occurrences which appear together to one observer may, without contradiction, appear as successive to another whose station is in motion with respect to him.
The instant which a distant occurrence is assigned depends upon the manner in which we have chosen to synchronise the clocks in that region of space.
Between two events separated by so wide an interval that no signal can pass from one to the other, no fact of nature determines which was the earlier.
That two flashes are contemporaneous is not a property residing in the flashes themselves, but a relation between them and an assumed standard of comparison.
The judgement of simultaneity, when applied to events at a distance, has no meaning apart from a prior convention as to the transport or synchronisation of clocks.
If our clocks be regulated by the exchange of luminous signals, the equality of the transit-times in either sense is a stipulation, and not a discovered fact.
Were the observer to change the state of motion of his laboratory, events which he formerly reckoned as coincident might come to be reckoned as unequal in date.
The time attributed to a distant event is not a natural datum, but a construction whose value alters with the frame from which the reckoning is undertaken.
There is no use in enquiring, of two remote occurrences beyond mutual influence, which of them was in truth the first, for no experiment can furnish a reply.
When two events are separated by more space than light can traverse between their epochs, their temporal order remains indeterminate for all conceivable observers.
The proposition that two distant occurrences take place together admits of no purely physical import until a rule for the setting of remote clocks has been assigned.
Two observers, moving one with respect to the other, may with equal justice each maintain that his own clocks are in step, though they disagree upon the fact.
There would appear that the customary notion of a single, universal instant embracing all of nature is an unwarranted extrapolation from immediate observer experience.
The order in time of events which lie beyond one another's reach by any physical signal is a matter of convention, and not of ascertainable fact.
That two occurrences should be judged coincident depends upon the criterion of coincidence adopted, and the criterion is itself an artefact of our own choice.
If two lanterns are extinguished at what one traveller declares to be the same moment, another traveller in relative motion may with equal right deny their coincidence.
There is no universal now such as former philosophers imagined, but only such coincidences of local events as our conventions of measurement permit us to construct.
The synchronisation of clocks at a distance rests upon a definition, and the definition may be altered without any conflict with the observed course of nature.
To assert that two events at opposite quarters of the heavens occur together is to assert nothing at all, until the rule of comparison has been specified.
